# Introduction {#intro}

```{r fig.align='center', echo=FALSE, out.width='100%', fig.cap='IOBRpy workflow'}
knitr::include_graphics('assets/img/IOBRpy.png', dpi = NA)
```

This tutorial presents a reproducible IOBRpy workflow that starts with public paired-end FASTQ files and continues through quality control, Salmon quantification, TPM preparation, tumor microenvironment profiling, ligand-receptor scoring, and TRUST4 repertoire analysis.

The chapter structure follows the practical style of the [RIMA tutorial](https://liulab-dfci.github.io/RIMA/): prepare the environment and inputs, run the main workflow, and inspect each output module. The commands here cover only functions currently provided by IOBRpy.

## What you will produce

The complete workflow creates:

```text
results/gbm-demo/
├── 01-qc/
├── 02-salmon/
├── 03-tpm/
├── 04-signatures/
├── 05-tme/
├── 06-LR_cal/
└── 07-TCRBCR/
```

By the end of the tutorial, you will be able to:

- obtain small paired-end FASTQ subsets from a public repository;
- build a Salmon index that matches the transcript FASTA;
- inspect inputs and validate workflow parameters with `map` and `recommend`;
- run FASTQ-to-TPM, TME, ligand-receptor, and TRUST4 analysis with `runall`;
- distinguish cell fractions, abundance scores, signatures, and exploratory outputs;
- replace the teaching data with your own FASTQ files.

## Teaching dataset

The example uses four pretreatment glioblastoma samples from [PRJNA482620](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA482620). This anti-PD-1 glioblastoma study is also used by the RIMA tutorial. The source study is [Zhao et al., Nature Medicine (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-019-0349-y).

| Run | Patient | Teaching group | Time point | Library |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| SRR8281218 | P20 | NR | Pre | paired-end RNA-seq |
| SRR8281226 | P53 | NR | Pre | paired-end RNA-seq |
| SRR8281245 | P100 | R | Pre | paired-end RNA-seq |
| SRR8281243 | P101 | R | Pre | paired-end RNA-seq |

The downloader does not save each complete source FASTQ file. It streams the first 50,000 complete records from each mate and then closes the network connection.

> **Teaching limitation:** Four samples with 50,000 read pairs each are suitable for learning file organization, command execution, and output structure. They do not support stable group-level inference or publication-quality immune infiltration and repertoire-diversity conclusions.

## Why the main workflow uses Salmon

IOBRpy `runall` supports both Salmon and STAR. Salmon is used here because the teaching goal is to complete expression quantification and downstream TME analysis with relatively modest resources.

STAR is more appropriate when explicit BAM files, genomic coordinates, or a count-based branch are required, but its genome index, memory, storage, and run-time requirements are higher. The final chapters show how to switch your own data to STAR mode.

## Conventions

- Commands are written for Bash on Linux, macOS, or WSL2.
- Expression matrices use **genes × samples** orientation.
- `iobrpy-cli` performs environment checks, path analysis, and parameter validation; installed IOBRpy native commands execute the workflow steps.
- Paths are relative to the `IOBRpy_book/` repository root.
